<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Two admissible histories \(h\) and \(h'\) are equivalent, written \(h\sim h'\), when
\begin{equation}
\Pr(\bm O=\bm o\mid h,\operatorname{do}(\bm A=\bm a))
=
\Pr(\bm O=\bm o\mid h',\operatorname{do}(\bm A=\bm a))
\label{eq:counterfactual-equivalence}
\end{equation}
for every finite future action string \(\bm a\) and every compatible future observation string \(\bm o\).
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:canonical-state}
The quotient \(\mathcal{S}_\epsilon\) has the following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item It is predictively sufficient for every finite intervention-conditioned future.
\item Its update is recursive: whenever \(hao\) is admissible, the map
\[
([h],a,o)\longmapsto[hao]
\]
is well defined.
\item It is minimal among exact counterfactual state representations.  If \(\phi(h)\) determines all probabilities in Eq.~\eqref{eq:counterfactual-equivalence}, then there exists a map \(g\) such that
\[
[h]=g(\phi(h)).
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Sufficiency is the definition of the equivalence classes.  For recursive update, let \(h\sim h'\) and suppose both extensions by \(a,o\) are admissible.  Conditional probabilities of every later test after \(hao\) are ratios of joint test probabilities after \(h\); equality of all joint probabilities for \(h\) and \(h'\) gives equality after conditioning.  Hence \(hao\sim h'ao\).  For minimality, if \(\phi(h)=\phi(h')\) while \(h\not\sim h'\), then some intervention-conditioned future probability differs, contradicting exactness of \(\phi\).  Therefore each level set of \(\phi\) lies within one predictive-equivalence class, and the quotient label is a function of \(\phi\).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
The matrix \(K=CLR\) is a valid continuous-time Markov generator on \(\Delta_m\).
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Column conservation follows from stochasticity:
\[
\mathbf{1}_m^\mathsf TK=\mathbf{1}_n^\mathsf TLR=0.
\]
For \(\alpha\neq\beta\), the identity
\[
0=(CR)_{\alpha\beta}
=\sum_i C_{\alpha i}R_{i\beta}
\]
and nonnegativity imply \(C_{\alpha i}R_{i\beta}=0\) termwise.  Therefore diagonal entries of \(L\) make no contribution to \(K_{\alpha\beta}\), while all off-diagonal contributions are nonnegative.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:defect}
For all \(s,t\ge0\),
\begin{equation}
T_{s+t}-T_sT_t
=
C\mathrm{e}^{sL}Q\mathrm{e}^{tL}R.
\label{eq:defect}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Insert \(I=P+Q\) between the two fine propagators:
\[
T_{s+t}=C\mathrm{e}^{sL}(P+Q)\mathrm{e}^{tL}R.
\]
The \(P\) term is
\[
C\mathrm{e}^{sL}RC\mathrm{e}^{tL}R=T_sT_t,
\]
leaving Eq.~\eqref{eq:defect}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:memory}
The coarse propagator satisfies
\begin{equation}
\dot T_t
=
KT_t+\int_0^t \mathcal{M}(\tau)T_{t-\tau}\,\,\mathrm{d}\tau,
\qquad T_0=I_m,
\label{eq:volterra}
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{M}(\tau)=A\mathrm{e}^{\tau H}B.
\label{eq:kernel}
\end{equation}
Its Laplace transform is
\begin{equation}
\widehat T(z)
=
\left[zI_m-K-A(zI-H)^{-1}B\right]^{-1}
\label{eq:resolvent}
\end{equation}
for sufficiently large \(\operatorname{Re}z\).
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Variation of constants gives
\[
\eta(t)=\int_0^t\mathrm{e}^{(t-s)H}Bq(s)\,\,\mathrm{d} s.
\]
Substitution into the equation for \(q\) yields Eq.~\eqref{eq:volterra}.  Laplace transformation gives
\[
z\widehat T-I=K\widehat T+\widehat{\mathcal{M}}\widehat T,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathcal{M}}(z)=A(zI-H)^{-1}B,
\]
and hence Eq.~\eqref{eq:resolvent}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:tomography}
The full sequence \(\{M_n\}_{n\ge0}\) is uniquely determined by \(\{S_n\}_{n\ge0}\).  Specifically,
\begin{equation}
S_{n+1}
=
KS_n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}M_jS_{n-1-j},
\qquad n\ge1,
\label{eq:recurrence}
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}
M_{n-1}
=
S_{n+1}-KS_n
-\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}M_jS_{n-1-j}.
\label{eq:tomography}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Expand
\[
T_t=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{S_n}{n!}t^n,
\qquad
\mathcal{M}(t)=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{M_j}{j!}t^j.
\]
The convolution term in Eq.~\eqref{eq:volterra} is
\begin{align}
\int_0^t\mathcal{M}(\tau)T_{t-\tau}\,\,\mathrm{d}\tau
&=
\sum_{j,k\ge0}
\frac{M_jS_k}{j!\,k!}
\int_0^t\tau^j(t-\tau)^k\,\,\mathrm{d}\tau\\
&=
\sum_{j,k\ge0}
M_jS_k\,\frac{t^{j+k+1}}{(j+k+1)!},
\end{align}
because the beta integral cancels the factorials.  Matching the coefficient of \(t^n/n!\) in Eq.~\eqref{eq:volterra} gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:recurrence}; solving for the newest moment gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:tomography}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The tomography requires a preparation protocol \(R\): after each trial, the same macrostate must be reset to the same fine distribution.  Without controlled preparation, passive trajectories mix dynamical memory with uncertainty about the within-fibre state.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The linear closure rank is
\begin{equation}
r_{\mathrm{cl}}=\operatorname{rank}\mathbb H_\infty.
\label{eq:closure-rank}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:minimal-completion}
Assume finite-dimensional fine dynamics as above.  Then:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item An exact linear auxiliary completion exists.
\item The minimum auxiliary dimension is \(r_{\mathrm{cl}}\).
\item Every minimal completion realizes the same memory moments,
\[
M_k=A_\star H_\star^kB_\star,
\]
and any two controllable and observable minimal completions are related by an invertible hidden-state similarity.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Existence of some finite completion follows from the microscopic triple \((A,H,B)\), whose effective dimension is at most \(\operatorname{rank} Q\).

For the lower bound, suppose Eq.~\eqref{eq:completion} of dimension \(r\) reproduces \(T_t\).  Eliminating \(z\) gives
\[
\mathcal{M}_\star(t)=A_\star\mathrm{e}^{tH_\star}B_\star.
\]
Equality of the resulting coarse resolvent with Eq.~\eqref{eq:resolvent} for all sufficiently large \(z\) implies equality of the memory transfer functions and hence
\[
M_k=A_\star H_\star^kB_\star
\quad (k\ge0).
\]
Every finite Hankel block then factors through an \(r\)-dimensional space:
\[
\mathbb H_{p,q}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A_\star\\A_\star H_\star\\ \vdots
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
B_\star&H_\star B_\star&\cdots
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus \(r_{\mathrm{cl}}\le r\).

For the matching upper bound, construct the state space directly from the infinite Hankel operator.  For \(j\ge0\) and \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\), let
\[
c_{j,u}:=(M_{i+j}u)_{i\ge0}
\]
be an infinite block column, and let
\[
\mathcal X=\operatorname{span}\{c_{j,u}:j\ge0,\ u\in\mathbb{R}^m\}.
\]
By definition, \(\dim\mathcal X=r_{\mathrm{cl}}\).  Define
\[
B_\star u=c_{0,u},\qquad
H_\star c_{j,u}=c_{j+1,u},
\]
and let \(A_\star:\mathcal X\to\mathbb{R}^m\) extract the zeroth block component.  The shift \(H_\star\) is well defined: if
\[
\sum_\alpha c_{j_\alpha,u_\alpha}=0,
\]
then for every \(i\ge0\),
\[
\sum_\alpha M_{i+j_\alpha}u_\alpha=0;
\]
replacing \(i\) by \(i+1\) proves
\[
\sum_\alpha c_{j_\alpha+1,u_\alpha}=0.
\]
By construction,
\[
A_\star H_\star^kB_\star u=M_ku
\]
for every \(k\) and \(u\).  Hence \((A_\star,H_\star,B_\star)\) realizes the full analytic memory kernel in dimension \(r_{\mathrm{cl}}\).  Substitution into Eq.~\eqref{eq:resolvent} shows that the augmented system reproduces \(T_t\) exactly.  The lower bound is therefore attained.

The constructed realization is reachable because \(\mathcal X\) is spanned by \(H_\star^kB_\star u\), and observable because a vector whose every block component \(A_\star H_\star^\ell x\) vanishes is the zero infinite column.  For two reachable and observable minimal realizations, mapping states generated by identical finite input sequences defines an invertible intertwiner \(S\), yielding
\[
H_2=SH_1S^{-1},\qquad
B_2=SB_1,\qquad
A_2=A_1S^{-1}.
\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:finite-tomography}
If \(r_{\mathrm{cl}}=r\), then some finite pair \(p,q\le r\) has stabilized Hankel rank \(r\), and the corresponding Hankel and shifted Hankel blocks determine a minimal completion.  In particular, the square choice \(p=q=r\) requires at most
\[
M_0,\ldots,M_{2r-1},
\]
which are recoverable from
\[
S_0,\ldots,S_{2r+1}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:closure}
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(r_{\mathrm{cl}}=0\);
\item \(\mathcal{M}(t)\equiv0\);
\item \(T_t=\mathrm{e}^{tK}\) for all \(t\ge0\);
\item \(T_{s+t}=T_sT_t\) for all \(s,t\ge0\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Zero Hankel rank is equivalent to \(M_k=0\) for every \(k\), hence to the vanishing analytic kernel.  The Volterra equation then reduces to \(\dot T=KT\).  Conversely, an exact semigroup has no memory self-energy in Eq.~\eqref{eq:resolvent}.  The last equivalence follows from differentiability and \(\dot T_0=K\).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:fisher}
If \(p(t)\) and \(r(t)\) are probability curves with \(p(0)=r(0)=q\) and
\[
p(t)-r(t)=\frac{t^\ell}{\ell!}v+O(t^{\ell+1}),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
D_f(p(t)\|r(t))
=
\frac{f''(1)}{2(\ell!)^2}
t^{2\ell}\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{F(q)}^2
+O(t^{2\ell+1}).
\label{eq:local-f}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Write \(\delta_i=p_i-r_i\).  Taylor expansion at equality gives
\[
D_f(p\|r)
=
\frac{f''(1)}2\sum_i\frac{\delta_i^2}{r_i}
+O(\left\lVert \delta\right\rVert^3).
\]
Since \(r_i=q_i+O(t)\), substitution of the assumed displacement yields Eq.~\eqref{eq:local-f}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:depth-law}
If \(d_\star<\infty\), then
\begin{equation}
T_t-\mathrm{e}^{tK}
=
\frac{t^{d_\star+2}}{(d_\star+2)!}M_{d_\star}
+O(t^{d_\star+3}).
\label{eq:path-depth}
\end{equation}
For every interior \(q\notin\operatorname{ker} M_{d_\star}\),
\begin{equation}
D_f(T_tq\|\mathrm{e}^{tK}q)
=
\frac{f''(1)t^{2d_\star+4}}
{2[(d_\star+2)!]^2}
\left\lVert M_{d_\star}q\right\rVert_{F(q)}^2
+O(t^{2d_\star+5}).
\label{eq:depth-law}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
In Eq.~\eqref{eq:volterra}, all kernel derivatives below order \(d_\star\) vanish, so
\[
\mathcal{M}(\tau)=\frac{\tau^{d_\star}}{d_\star!}M_{d_\star}
+O(\tau^{d_\star+1}).
\]
At leading order \(T_{t-\tau}=I+O(t)\).  Integrating once in the Volterra equation gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:path-depth}; Lemma~\ref{lem:fisher} gives Eq.~\eqref{eq:depth-law}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let \(r_+\) be the minimum number of auxiliary probability coordinates in any finite Markov realization whose coarse response is \(T_t\).
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- principle-1: body_md -->
A description is dynamically complete over an operational domain exactly when its present state is sufficient for every admissible future intervention and readout.  When it is incomplete, the physically relevant missing state is the minimal extension that restores this sufficiency; coordinate choices inside that extension have no independent operational meaning.
<!-- end principle-1 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:robust-closure-rank}
Let \(\mathbb H_{p,q}\) be a finite memory-Hankel block and let
\(\widehat{\mathbb H}_{p,q}\) obey
\[
 \|\widehat{\mathbb H}_{p,q}-\mathbb H_{p,q}\|_2\le\varepsilon.
\]
If \(\widehat\sigma_k>\varepsilon\), then every exact autonomous linear
completion has auxiliary dimension at least \(k\).  If the infinite
memory-Hankel operator has rank \(r\), the chosen finite block already has
rank \(r\), and
\[
 \sigma_r(\mathbb H_{p,q})>2\varepsilon,
\]
then every threshold in
\((\varepsilon,\sigma_r-\varepsilon)\) recovers the exact minimal
completion dimension.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Weyl's inequality gives
\[
 |\widehat\sigma_j-\sigma_j|\le\varepsilon.
\]
Thus \(\widehat\sigma_k>\varepsilon\) forces
\(\sigma_k>0\), and the Hankel-rank minimality theorem gives the lower
bound.  Under the second hypothesis,
\(\widehat\sigma_r\ge\sigma_r-\varepsilon\) and
\(\widehat\sigma_{r+1}\le\varepsilon\), which proves exact recovery.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:frontier-holonomy-samples}
Let a scalar \(p\times q\) memory-Hankel block be estimated entrywise,
using \(N\) independent observations in \([0,1]\) for each entry.  With
probability at least \(1-\delta\),
\[
 \|\widehat{\mathbb H}-\mathbb H\|_2
 \le
 \sqrt{\frac{pq}{2N}\log\frac{2pq}{\delta}}
 =:\varepsilon_N.
\]
Consequently every \(\widehat\sigma_k>\varepsilon_N\) certifies at least
\(k\) hidden predictive coordinates.  If the true block has rank \(r\)
and smallest nonzero singular value \(\sigma_r\), then
\[
 N>
 \frac{2pq}{\sigma_r^2}\log\frac{2pq}{\delta}
\]
is sufficient for exact rank recovery by a threshold between
\(\varepsilon_N\) and \(\sigma_r-\varepsilon_N\).
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Hoeffding's inequality and a union bound control every entry by
\(\sqrt{\log(2pq/\delta)/(2N)}\).  The operator norm is at most the
Frobenius norm, giving \(\varepsilon_N\).  The robust closure-rank theorem
then applies; the sample inequality is exactly \(2\varepsilon_N<\sigma_r\).
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:final-holonomy-matrix-bernstein}
Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\) be independent \(p\times q\) random matrices with
\(\mathbb EZ_s=\mathbb H\), and put \(X_s=Z_s-\mathbb H\).  Suppose
\(\|X_s\|_2\le L\) almost surely and define
\[
 v=\max\left\{
 \left\|\sum_{s=1}^N\mathbb E X_sX_s^*\right\|_2,
 \left\|\sum_{s=1}^N\mathbb E X_s^*X_s\right\|_2
 \right\}.
\]
Then, with probability at least \(1-\delta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left\|\frac1N\sum_{s=1}^NZ_s-\mathbb H\right\|_2
 &\le
 \frac{\sqrt{2v\log((p+q)/\delta)}}{N}\\
 &\quad+\frac{2L\log((p+q)/\delta)}{3N}
 =:\varepsilon_{\rm MB}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every empirical singular value above \(\varepsilon_{\rm MB}\) certifies a
hidden predictive coordinate, and
\(2\varepsilon_{\rm MB}<\sigma_r(\mathbb H)\) guarantees exact recovery of
rank \(r\).
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Rectangular matrix Bernstein gives the displayed operator-norm deviation
for the empirical average.  Weyl's singular-value perturbation inequality
then shifts every singular value by at most
\(\varepsilon_{\rm MB}\), exactly as in the robust closure-rank theorem.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
